finding.statement: The inventory is complete only when every instrument has been run for a father John Gurney and for each of the children Mary, Richard and John, variant-expanded, across 1615-1645 for England and Wales; positive controls pass on every instrument; every returned row is catalogued with its provenance and a household id; every household is scored with its shape hypothesis and discriminating evidence recorded; a coverage statement exists per county worked; and the residual is named as a list of parishes whose registers are known lost for 1620-1640, so the unsearchable remainder is a stated quantity rather than an unknown. Eight self-checks enforce it. Read the project's own record first, including the source registry. Run a positive control on every sweep - a query that does not return a record already known to exist and in scope is broken, and its result is not a finding. Match the place token to the target set rather than to the parish's name, because a keyword filter is a literal token match that fails closed. Check that the surname stem actually reaches the spelling in use, since a wildcard covers one stem and is not a variant sweep. Never combine a year bound with a place keyword in a single-dataset query: the combination fails closed, proven by 349 baptisms at one parish with no year bound and zero with a year bound in a set that demonstrably holds a baptism in that year under another surname - and any negative in the existing record resting on both parameters at once is void and must be re-run. Pre-register the expected order of magnitude. Record no negative from one provider alone, since no index is complete and the gaps do not coincide. Ask every question by child, by parent and by place. Weight the variant and never exclude a surname as a class. Weight against shape rather than volume. Enumerate shapes before collapsing a household to one. Stop and rebuild the method after two corrections in the same domain. And treat a finding without an instrument code and a query date as not a finding.

sources.locator: sid=102 parent search, fatherfirstname=john and fatherlastname=gurney both variant-expanded, collection=parish+baptisms, sourcecountry=great+britain, yearofbirth=1630&yearofbirth_offset=5, 28 July 2026: facet panel reports Parish Baptisms 108, Parish Burials 76, Parish Marriages 13, Wills & Probate 0; year=1630&year_offset=10 returns 0 while rendering a chip

finding.statement: The natural inversion of the search - which John Gurney household's records stop between 1635 and 1641 without a burial or probate for the head - has been treated as something to do parish by parish. It is not. The parent-name search runs over burials as well as baptisms: a father-John-Gurney sweep for 1625-1635 reports, in one facet panel, 108 parish baptisms, 76 parish burials and 13 parish marriages. Switching the collection to parish burials therefore asks in a single query which children of a John Gurney were buried in England, and the households appearing in the baptism arm but not the burial arm are exactly the departure-shaped gaps. Two mechanics have to be right first: the year parameter in this mode must be the birth-year form, because the plain year parameter renders a filter chip and then returns a silent zero; and the pool excludes some county sets, so the burial arm needs pairing with county-set runs exactly as the baptism arm does. This is the highest-value single query left on the child inventory and it has never been executed - which is the wider point the method was written for: this work has repeatedly gained more from establishing that an instrument said what it appeared to say than from running more searches.
